claim: Thirteen healthy German native speakers (6 females; 7 males; mean age: 24.8 years, standard deviation: 1.5 years, range: 22–27 years) participated in the fMRI study.
source: Thirteen healthy German native speakers (6 females; 7 males; mean age: 24.8 years, standard deviation: 1.5 years, range: 22–27 years) gave written informed consent to participate in this fMRI study.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the manuscript.

claim: Two subjects did not complete all fMRI sessions and were excluded from analysis.
source: Two of those subjects did not complete all fMRI sessions and were therefore not included in the analysis.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Leipzig.
source: All procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Leipzig.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: The visual looming stimulus had a duration of 500 ms.
source: The visual looming stimulus (500 ms duration) was a sequence of 1 to 4 radially expanding white annuli (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus duration.

claim: The auditory looming stimulus had a duration of 500 ms.
source: The auditory looming stimulus (500 ms duration) was composed of several pure tones (55, 110, 150, 220, 330, 380, 440, 660, 880, 990, 1110, 1500, 2500, 3000 Hz) that increased in frequency and amplitude over the entire 500 ms duration.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus duration.

claim: The auditory looming stimulus was composed of pure tones at frequencies 55, 110, 150, 220, 330, 380, 440, 660, 880, 990, 1110, 1500, 2500, 3000 Hz.
source: The auditory looming stimulus (500 ms duration) was composed of several pure tones (55, 110, 150, 220, 330, 380, 440, 660, 880, 990, 1110, 1500, 2500, 3000 Hz) that increased in frequency and amplitude over the entire 500 ms duration.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus composition.

claim: The mixture of sound frequencies in the auditory looming stimulus ensured widespread activations in auditory cortices due to tonotopic organization.
source: Given the tonotopic organization of primary auditory cortices (Formisano et al., 2003) this mixture of sound frequencies ensured widespread activations in auditory cortices.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work on tonotopic organization.

claim: The visual looming parameters ensured relatively widespread activations in visual cortices due to retinotopic organization.
source: Given the retinotopic organization of early visual cortices (Wandell et al., 2007) these parameters ensured that visual looming elicited relatively widespread activations in visual cortices.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work on retinotopic organization.

claim: The experiment used a 3 (stimulus modality: auditory, visual, audiovisual) X 2 (attended modality: auditory, visual) factorial design.
source: The experiment conformed to a 3 (stimulus modality: auditory, visual, audiovisual) X 2 (attended modality: auditory, visual) factorial design (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design with reference to figure.

claim: Looming stimuli were used as biologically relevant and highly salient stimuli that reliably evoke crossmodal influences in sensory cortices.
source: We used looming motion as a biologically relevant and highly salient stimulus that reliably evokes crossmodal influences in sensory cortices in human neuroimaging and animal neurophysiology (Cappe et al., 2012; Maier et al., 2008; Tyll et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Participants were instructed to respond selectively to weak auditory or visual targets adjusted to threshold performance.
source: Modality-specific attention was manipulated by requiring participants to detect and respond selectively to weak auditory or visual targets, which were adjusted prior to the main study to threshold performance in sound amplitude or visual size for each participant.
evidence: Direct statement about task requirements.

claim: Activation blocks lasted 33 seconds.
source: Auditory, visual or audiovisual looming stimuli were presented in 33 s blocks of 50 stimuli (stimulus duration: 500 ms, inter-stimuli interval: 160 ms giving a fixed stimulus onset asynchrony of 660 ms with no jitter) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement about block duration.

claim: Activation blocks were preceded by 16 s fixation baseline periods.
source: Activation blocks were preceded by 16 s fixation baseline periods.
evidence: Direct statement about baseline duration.

claim: Each fMRI run included 18 blocks and lasted 15 minutes.
source: Each fMRI run included 18 blocks (three blocks for each condition in our 2 × 3 design) and lasted 15 min.
evidence: Direct statement about run structure.

claim: There were four runs per participant yielding 12 blocks per condition per participant.
source: There were four runs per participant yielding 12 blocks per condition per participant.
evidence: Direct statement about total number of runs and blocks.

claim: There was a significant main effect of attended modality on target response percentages (F(1, 10)=291.263, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.967).
source: We observed significant main effects of attended modality (F(1, 10)=291.263, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.967), target modality (F(1, 10)=13.289, p=0.004, ηp2 = 0.571), and stimulus modality (F(1.986, 19.864)=5.304, p=0.014, ηp2 = 0.347), together with a significant interaction between target modality and attended modality (F(1, 10)=14.786, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.597).
evidence: Statistical test results from behavioral data analysis.

claim: There was a significant interaction between target modality and attended modality (F(1, 10)=14.786, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.597), confirming that participants successfully maintained auditory or visual attention as instructed.
source: This interaction confirmed that participants had successfully maintained auditory or visual attention as instructed.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical result from behavioral data.

claim: Hit rates for auditory targets under auditory attention were greater than for visual targets under visual attention during auditory blocks (t(10)=2.845, p=0.017, Hedges gav = 0.804).
source: These interactions resulted from greater hit rates for auditory targets given auditory attention than for visual targets given visual attention during both auditory (t(10)=2.845, p=0.017, Hedges gav = 0.804) and visual blocks (t(10)=4.432, p=0.001, Hedges gav = 2.037), but not for audio-visual blocks (t(10)=0.276, p=0.788, Hedges gav = 0.081) suggesting that observers' performance was not completely matched across all conditions.
evidence: Statistical test results from behavioral data analysis.

claim: The presentation of auditory and visual stimuli in audiovisual blocks interfered with the detection of auditory targets.
source: Specifically, the presentation of auditory and visual stimuli in the audiovisual blocks interfered with the detection of auditory targets.
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral results.

claim: The study used submillimeter-resolution fMRI at 7T.
source: Using sub-millimeter-resolution fMRI at 7T, we resolved BOLD-response and activation patterns across cortical depth in early sensory cortices to auditory, visual and audiovisual stimuli under auditory or visual attention.
evidence: Direct statement about imaging methodology in abstract.

claim: All experiments were performed on a Siemens 7T MAGNETOM MRI scanner.
source: All experiments were performed on a Siemens 7T MAGNETOM MRI scanner (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with an SC72 gradient coil (Siemens Healthineers).
evidence: Direct statement about scanner specifications.

claim: A single-channel-transmit/32-channel-receive phased array head coil was used for radio-frequency transmission and reception.
source: For radio-frequency transmission and reception, a single-channel-transmit/32-channel-receive phased array head coil (Nova Medical, Wilmington, MA) was used.
evidence: Direct statement about coil specifications.

claim: The first six volumes in each run were automatically discarded to avoid T1 saturation effects.
source: The first six volumes in each run were automatically discarded to avoid for T1 saturation effects.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: A whole-brain MP2RAGE sequence was used to acquire a quantitative T1 map.
source: On the first day a whole-brain MP2RAGE sequence (Marques et al., 2010) was used to acquire a quantitative T1 map and a weighted T1 image and a second inversion image to enable high-resolution segmentation and cortical laminae definition [repetition time (TR)/echo time (TE) = 5000/2.45 ms, inversion time 1 = 900 ms, flip angle 1 = 5°, inversion time 2 = 2750 ms, flip angle 2 = 3°, 240 slices, matrix = 320 × 320, acquisition time = 600 s, spatial resolution = 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 mm3 voxels, partial Fourier factor = 6/8, parallel imaging using GRAPPA with an acceleration factor of 4, field of view = 168×224 mm].
evidence: Direct statement about structural imaging with citation.

claim: The T1 map spatial resolution was 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 mm3 voxels.
source: On the first day a whole-brain MP2RAGE sequence (Marques et al., 2010) was used to acquire a quantitative T1 map and a weighted T1 image and a second inversion image to enable high-resolution segmentation and cortical laminae definition [repetition time (TR)/echo time (TE) = 5000/2.45 ms, inversion time 1 = 900 ms, flip angle 1 = 5°, inversion time 2 = 2750 ms, flip angle 2 = 3°, 240 slices, matrix = 320 × 320, acquisition time = 600 s, spatial resolution = 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 mm3 voxels, partial Fourier factor = 6/8, parallel imaging using GRAPPA with an acceleration factor of 4, field of view = 168×224 mm].
evidence: Direct statement about structural imaging resolution.

claim: The T1 map was coregistered to Montreal's Neurological Institute brain space and resampled to an isometric resolution of 0.4 mm.
source: The T1 map was coregistered to the Montreal's Neurological Institute brain space (rigid body registration and normalized mutual information as a cost function) and resampled to an isometric resolution of 0.4 mm.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: Six intracortical surfaces were computed between cortical boundary surfaces using the equivolume approach.
source: Between these surfaces, we computed six intracortical surfaces that defined cortical laminae with the equivolume approach (Waehnert et al., 2014) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement about laminar surface computation with citation.

claim: The term 'lamina' used in this study does not directly refer to cytoarchitectonically defined cortical layers.
source: It is important to note that the term 'lamina' used in this communication does not directly refer to cytoarchitectonically defined cortical layers: for example, the variation across cortical regions of the relative thickness between layers was not modelled here (Nieuwenhuys, 2013).
evidence: Direct statement clarifying terminology with citation.

claim: The equivolume method provides biologically plausible cortical contours.
source: However, it should be mentioned that this method provides biologically plausible cortical contours (Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Four regions of interest were defined: primary auditory cortex (A1), planum temporale (PT), primary visual cortex (V1), and higher order visual cortex (V2/3).
source: We defined four regions of interest (ROI), each combining left and right hemispheres, as follows (see Table S2 for ROI effective sizes):
evidence: Direct statement about ROI definition.

claim: Coverage was >95% for A1, PT and V1 and >82% for V2/3.
source: We obtained >95% coverage for A1, PT and V1 and >82% coverage for V2/3. (For the number of vertices and percentage coverage across subjects, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct statement about ROI coverage.

claim: fMRI data were preprocessed and analyzed using SPM12.
source: The fMRI data were pre-processed and analyzed using statistical parametric mapping (SPM12 – v6685; Wellcome Center for Neuroimaging, London, UK; www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm; RRID:SCR_007037) running on matlab (Mathworks).
evidence: Direct statement about analysis software.

claim: A mixed block-event related model was used with regressors convolved with a canonical hemodynamic response function and its temporal derivative.
source: We modelled the fMRI experiment with a mixed block-event related model with regressors entered into the run-specific design matrix after convolving the onsets of each block or event with a canonical hemodynamic response function (HRF) and its temporal derivative.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM modeling approach.

claim: In visual cortices, auditory stimulation induced widespread inhibition irrespective of attention.
source: In visual cortices, auditory stimulation induced widespread inhibition irrespective of attention, whereas auditory relative to visual attention suppressed mainly central visual field representations.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: Auditory relative to visual attention suppressed mainly central visual field representations in visual cortices.
source: In visual cortices, auditory stimulation induced widespread inhibition irrespective of attention, whereas auditory relative to visual attention suppressed mainly central visual field representations.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: In auditory cortices, visual stimulation suppressed activations.
source: In auditory cortices, visual stimulation suppressed activations, but amplified responses to concurrent auditory stimuli, in a patchy topography.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: In auditory cortices, visual stimulation amplified responses to concurrent auditory stimuli in a patchy topography.
source: In auditory cortices, visual stimulation suppressed activations, but amplified responses to concurrent auditory stimuli, in a patchy topography.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: Multisensory interactions in auditory cortices were stronger in deeper laminae.
source: Critically, multisensory interactions in auditory cortices were stronger in deeper laminae, while attentional influences were greatest at the surface.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: Attentional influences in auditory cortices were greatest at the surface.
source: Critically, multisensory interactions in auditory cortices were stronger in deeper laminae, while attentional influences were greatest at the surface.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in abstract.

claim: The distinct depth-dependent profiles suggest that multisensory and attentional mechanisms regulate sensory processing via partly distinct circuitries.
source: These distinct depth-dependent profiles suggest that multisensory and attentional mechanisms regulate sensory processing via partly distinct circuitries.
evidence: Direct interpretation of findings in abstract.

claim: Mounting evidence suggests that interactions across the senses are pervasive in neocortex, arising even in primary cortices.
source: Mounting evidence from neuroimaging (Beauchamp et al., 2004; Noesselt et al., 2007; Rohe and Noppeney, 2016), neurophysiology (Atilgan et al., 2018; Kayser et al., 2010; Kayser et al., 2008; Lakatos et al., 2007) and neuroanatomy (Falchier et al., 2002; Rockland and Ojima, 2003) suggests that interactions across the senses are pervasive in neocortex, arising even in primary cortices (Driver and Noesselt, 2008; Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Liang et al., 2013; Schroeder and Foxe, 2002).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: fMRI in humans has shown that visual stimuli can induce crossmodal deactivations in primary and secondary auditory cortices.
source: Most prominently, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in humans has shown that visual stimuli can induce crossmodal deactivations in primary and secondary auditory cortices (Laurienti et al., 2002; Leitão et al., 2013; Mozolic et al., 2008), yet enhance the response to a concurrent auditory stimulus (Werner and Noppeney, 2011; Werner and Noppeney, 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual stimuli can enhance the response to a concurrent auditory stimulus in auditory cortices.
source: Most prominently, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in humans has shown that visual stimuli can induce crossmodal deactivations in primary and secondary auditory cortices (Laurienti et al., 2002; Leitão et al., 2013; Mozolic et al., 2008), yet enhance the response to a concurrent auditory stimulus (Werner and Noppeney, 2011; Werner and Noppeney, 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurophysiological research has suggested that multisensory influences emerge early in sensory cortices and are to some extent preserved in anaesthetized animals.
source: Further, neurophysiological research has suggested that multisensory influences emerge early in sensory cortices and are to some extent preserved in anaesthetized animals (Butler et al., 2012; Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012; Kayser et al., 2007; Mercier et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ability to extrapolate from neurophysiological findings in animals to human fMRI studies is limited by the nature of the BOLD response.
source: Yet, the ability to extrapolate from neurophysiological findings in animals to human fMRI studies is limited by the nature of the BOLD response, which pools neural activity over time and across a vast number of neurons (Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Statement about methodological limitation with citation.

claim: Both multisensory and attentional mechanisms enhance perceptual sensitivity.
source: Critically, multisensory and attentional mechanisms are closely intertwined. Both enhance perceptual sensitivity (Leo et al., 2011) and precision of sensory representations (Ernst and Bülthoff, 2004; Fetsch et al., 2012; Meijer et al., 2019; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The co-occurrence of two congruent sensory stimuli boosts the salience of an event, which may attract greater attention.
source: Most importantly, the co-occurrence of two congruent sensory stimuli boosts the salience of an event (Lewis and Noppeney, 2010; Van der Burg et al., 2008), which may thereby attract greater attention.
evidence: Statement supported by citations with inference about attention.

claim: Shifting attention endogenously to one sensory modality reduces processing and activations in the unattended sensory systems.
source: Behavioural and functional imaging studies have shown that shifting attention endogenously to one sensory modality reduces processing and activations in the unattended sensory systems (Ciaramitaro et al., 2007; Johnson and Zatorre, 2005; Mozolic et al., 2008; Rohe and Noppeney, 2018; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015; Shomstein and Yantis, 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The influence of visual stimuli on auditory cortices was shown to be enhanced when attention was focused on the visual sense.
source: Most prominently, the influence of visual stimuli on auditory cortices was shown to be enhanced when attention was focused on the visual sense (Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Previous neurophysiological studies have revealed influences of modality-specific attention predominantly in superficial laminae in non-human primates.
source: While previous neurophysiological studies have revealed influences of modality-specific attention predominantly in superficial laminae in non-human primates (Lakatos et al., 2009), visual influences on auditory cortices have recently been shown to be most prominent in deep layer 6 of auditory cortex in rodents (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual influences on auditory cortices have been shown to be most prominent in deep layer 6 of auditory cortex in rodents.
source: While previous neurophysiological studies have revealed influences of modality-specific attention predominantly in superficial laminae in non-human primates (Lakatos et al., 2009), visual influences on auditory cortices have recently been shown to be most prominent in deep layer 6 of auditory cortex in rodents (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Combined neurophysiological evidence from primates and rodents suggests a double dissociation of attentional and multisensory influences.
source: In other words, combined neurophysiological evidence from primates and rodents suggests a double disassociation of attentional and multisensory influences.
evidence: Inference from cited previous research.

claim: GE-EPI BOLD fMRI is not yet able to attribute activations unequivocally to specific cortical layers.
source: While gradient-echo echo-planar-imaging (GE-EPI) BOLD fMRI is not yet able to attribute activations unequivocally to specific cortical layers (Duong et al., 2003; Goense et al., 2012; Harel et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2017; Markuerkiaga et al., 2016; Trampel et al., 2019), the observation in the same cortical territories of distinct laminar activation profiles induced by multisensory and attentional influences would strongly imply distinct neural mechanisms.
evidence: Statement about methodological limitation with citations.

claim: Distinct laminar activation profiles induced by multisensory and attentional influences in the same cortical territories would strongly imply distinct neural mechanisms.
source: While gradient-echo echo-planar-imaging (GE-EPI) BOLD fMRI is not yet able to attribute activations unequivocally to specific cortical layers (Duong et al., 2003; Goense et al., 2012; Harel et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2017; Markuerkiaga et al., 2016; Trampel et al., 2019), the observation in the same cortical territories of distinct laminar activation profiles induced by multisensory and attentional influences would strongly imply distinct neural mechanisms.
evidence: Logical inference about interpretation of results.

claim: Auditory stimuli evoked a positive BOLD response in primary auditory cortex and especially in anterior portions of the planum temporale.
source: Auditory stimuli evoked a positive BOLD response in primary auditory cortex and especially in anterior portions of the planum temporale (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B and 3 right).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figures.

claim: The positive BOLD signal increased roughly linearly towards the cortical surface as expected from the typical physiological point spread function of the GE-EPI BOLD signal.
source: As expected from the typical physiological point spread function of the GE-EPI BOLD signal, the positive BOLD signal increased roughly linearly towards the cortical surface (Markuerkiaga et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Statement of result with citation and reference to figures.

claim: Deactivations induced by crossmodal visual stimuli were observed in both A1 and PT with a constant response profile.
source: Deactivations induced by crossmodal visual stimuli (i.e. a negative BOLD response for [V-Fix]) were observed in both A1 and PT with a constant response profile and based on visual inspection even a trend towards stronger deactivations in deeper laminae (Figure 2A left, Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure and table.

claim: Visually induced deactivations in auditory cortices were generally observed for both auditory and visual attention conditions, with no significant difference between them.
source: These visually induced deactivations were generally observed for both auditory and visual attention conditions, with no significant difference between them ([AttA-AttV] for visual stimuli in A1 and PT: F(2,40) = 0.644, p=0.530).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result.

claim: No significant crossmodulatory effect of visual stimuli on the BOLD-response in A1 and PT was observed in the context of concurrent auditory stimuli.
source: We did not observe a significant crossmodulatory effect of visual stimuli on the BOLD-response in A1 and PT in the context of concurrent auditory stimuli (Figure 3A left, Table 2A).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure and table.

claim: Pattern classifiers succeeded in discriminating between patterns elicited by [AV vs. A] conditions across all laminae in both PT and A1.
source: However, pattern classifiers succeeded in discriminating between patterns elicited by [AV vs. A] conditions across all laminae in both PT and A1 (Figure 3A right, Table 2B).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure and table.

claim: The visual stimulus changed the activation pattern elicited by a concurrent auditory stimulus even when the mean BOLD response did not differ significantly.
source: Thus, even when the mean BOLD response across vertices averaged across A1 and PT did not differ significantly for AV and A stimuli at a particular depth, the visual stimulus changed the activation pattern elicited by a concurrent auditory stimulus.
evidence: Interpretation of multivariate pattern analysis results.

claim: Sub-regions with crossmodal enhancement and suppression co-exist in A1 and PT.
source: This provides evidence that sub-regions with crossmodal enhancement and suppression co-exist in A1 and PT.
evidence: Inference from pattern classification results.

claim: Visual induced changes in activation patterns in auditory cortices were not significantly affected by modality-specific attention.
source: The visual induced changes in activation patterns were again not significantly affected by modality-specific attention (for the classification [AV-V]att A VS [AV-V]att V, F(2,40) = 0.185, p=0.832).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result.

claim: Salient visual looming stimuli affected auditory cortices irrespective of the direction of modality-specific attention in both unisensory and audiovisual contexts.
source: Taken together these results suggest that salient visual looming stimuli affected auditory cortices irrespective of the direction of modality-specific attention in both unisensory and audiovisual contexts.
evidence: Summary interpretation of results.

claim: Visual stimuli influenced activation patterns in auditory cortices in a patchy topography during unisensory visual and audiovisual contexts.
source: We next explored whether visual stimuli influenced activation patterns in auditory cortices in a similar patchy topography during unisensory visual and audiovisual contexts.
evidence: Statement of analysis objective based on observed patterns.

claim: In PT, the constant parameter for [V-Fix] predicted the constant for [AV-A]: the less a vertex is deactivated by visual stimuli in a unisensory context, the more it shows a visually induced enhancement of the response to a concurrent auditory stimulus.
source: In PT, the constant parameter for [V-Fix] predicted the constant for [AV-A]: the less a vertex is deactivated in PT by visual stimuli in a unisensory context, the more it shows a visually induced enhancement of the response to a concurrent auditory stimulus (constant: t(10)=3.460, p=0.006, linear: t(10)=1.853, p=0.094, see Figure 3Bi right).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result with interpretation.

claim: In A1, vertices with less deactivations in deeper relative to superficial laminae in unisensory visual context showed a robust crossmodal enhancement that was most pronounced in deeper laminae.
source: More interestingly, in A1 the linear shape parameter for [V-Fix] predicted the linear shape parameter of [AV-A]: vertices with less deactivations in deeper relative to superficial laminae in unisensory visual context showed a robust crossmodal enhancement that was most pronounced in deeper laminae (linear: t(10)=3.121, p=0.011, constant: t(10)=0.021, p=0.983, Figure 3Bii right).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result with interpretation.

claim: Visual stimuli generate a BOLD response in primary auditory cortex with a patchy topography similar for unisensory and audiovisual contexts.
source: These results strongly suggest that visual stimuli generate a BOLD response in primary auditory cortex with a patchy topography similar for unisensory and audiovisual contexts.
evidence: Interpretation of regression analysis results.

claim: The control analysis for [V-Fix] and [A-Fix] contrasts in auditory areas did not reveal any significant relationship between the two contrasts.
source: However, as shown in the raster plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 this control analysis did not reveal any significant relationship between the two contrasts.
evidence: Direct statement of control analysis result.

claim: The absence of a significant effect in the control analysis suggests that the similarity in topography between visually induced deactivations and cross-modal modulations reflects similarities in neural organization rather than non-specific effects.
source: The absence of a significant effect in this control analysis thus suggests that the similarity in topography between visually induced deactivations and cross-modal modulations reflects similarities in neural organization rather than non-specific effects.
evidence: Interpretation of control analysis result.

claim: Attentional modulation was greatest at the cortical surface in both A1 and PT for the regional BOLD response.
source: In contrast to these multisensory influences, attentional modulation was greatest at the cortical surface in both A1 and PT for the regional BOLD response (i.e. significant positive linear effect in A1 and PT, Figure 4Ai left, Table 3A).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure and table.

claim: Pattern classifiers discriminated between the auditory and visual attention conditions averaged across A1 and PT.
source: Averaged across A1 and PT, pattern classifiers also discriminated between the auditory and visual attention conditions (Figure 4Ai right, Table 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure and table.

claim: The decoding accuracy profiles for attention were characterized by a significant constant term and a non-significant trend for the linear term.
source: The decoding accuracy profiles were characterized by a significant constant term and a non-significant trend for the linear term.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result.

claim: The average similarity between auditory and visual attention conditions in A1 was greater than the average similarity between A and AV conditions.
source: The average similarity between auditory and visual attention conditions was indeed greater than the average similarity between A and AV conditions (two-sided exact sign permutation test on Fisher transformed correlation coefficients, p=0.008).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result.

claim: Auditory attention mainly scales the BOLD response in A1 whilst preserving the activation pattern, whereas visual stimuli alter the activation pattern in A1.
source: These results suggest that auditory attention mainly scales the BOLD response in A1 whilst preserving the activation pattern, whereas visual stimuli alter the activation pattern in A1.
evidence: Interpretation of similarity analysis results.

claim: Visual stimuli induced deactivations with a constant profile both in A1 and PT.
source: Visual stimuli induced deactivations with a constant profile both in A1 and PT.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: Visual inputs altered the activation pattern with a similar patchy topography in A1 and PT when presented alone or together with an auditory stimulus.
source: In fact, in A1 and PT visual inputs altered the activation pattern with a similar patchy topography when presented alone (i.e. visual-induced deactivation) or together with an auditory stimulus (i.e. crossmodal modulation).
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: Modality-specific attention amplified the mean BOLD-signal within A1 and PT mainly at the cortical surface.
source: Modality-specific attention amplified the mean BOLD-signal within A1 and PT mainly at the cortical surface (i.e. significant linear parameter).
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: In V1 and V2/3 visual stimuli induced activations that increased toward the cortical surface as expected for GE-EPI BOLD.
source: In V1 and V2/3 visual stimuli induced activations that increased toward the cortical surface as expected for GE-EPI BOLD (Markuerkiaga et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 left and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of result with citation.

claim: The study did not observe a more selective increase in activations for layer 4 in V1.
source: Contrary to previous research (Chen et al., 2013; Koopmans et al., 2010), we did not observe a more selective increase in activations for layer 4.
evidence: Direct statement of result with citations to previous research.

claim: The centrally presented visual looming stimuli activated predominantly areas representing the centre of the visual field with response suppressions in adjacent areas.
source: Consistent with previous research (Shmuel et al., 2002; Silver et al., 2008; Tootell et al., 1998), the centrally presented visual looming stimuli activated predominantly areas representing the centre of the visual field with response suppressions (i.e. negative BOLD) in adjacent areas (see dashed white lines in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B right).
evidence: Direct statement of result with citations to previous research.

claim: Auditory deactivations in visual cortices were not confined to the central field that was activated by visual stimuli but were particularly pronounced in the rostral part of the calcarine sulcus representing more eccentric positions of the visual field.
source: By contrast, auditory deactivations were not confined to the central field that was activated by visual stimuli. Instead, they were particularly pronounced in the rostral part of the calcarine sulcus representing more eccentric positions of the visual field (Figure 2B right and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 right).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figures.

claim: Auditory looming stimuli induced deactivations that increased in absolute magnitude toward the cortical surface.
source: Furthermore, auditory looming stimuli induced deactivations that increased in absolute magnitude toward the cortical surface (significant constant and linear effect, Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to table.

claim: Auditory deactivations in visual cortices were not significantly modulated by modality-specific attention.
source: Again as in auditory areas, these auditory deactivations were not significantly modulated by modality-specific attention ([AttV-AttA] for auditory stimuli in V1 and V2/3: F(2,40) = 1.651, p=0.205).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result.

claim: No significant cross-modal modulation of the regional BOLD response in V1 and V2/3 was observed.
source: Despite the pronounced deactivations elicited by unisensory auditory stimuli, we did not observe any significant cross-modal modulation of the regional BOLD response in V1 and V2/3 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 left and Supplementary file 4A).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to figure.

claim: Support vector classifiers were not able to discriminate between activation patterns for [AV vs. V] stimuli better than chance in visual cortices.
source: Likewise, the support vector classifiers were not able to discriminate between activation patterns for [AV vs. V] stimuli better than chance.
evidence: Direct statement of result.

claim: The effect of auditory stimuli on visual cortices was abolished under concurrent visual stimulation both in terms of regional BOLD response and activation patterns.
source: In summary, the effect of auditory stimuli on visual cortices was abolished under concurrent visual stimulation both in terms of regional BOLD response and activation patterns (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 right and Supplementary file 4B).
evidence: Summary statement of result with reference to figure.

claim: No significant differences in mean BOLD responses in V1 or V2/3 were observed for visual vs. auditory attention conditions.
source: With respect to attentional modulation, we observed no significant differences in mean BOLD responses in V1 or V2/3 for visual vs. auditory attention conditions (see Table 3A).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to table.

claim: The classifier was able to discriminate between patterns for visual and auditory attention conditions successfully across all cortical depth surfaces in V1 and V2/3.
source: Yet, the classifier was able to discriminate between patterns for visual and auditory attention conditions successfully across all cortical depth surfaces in V1 and V2/3 (i.e. significant constant term in V1 and V2/3 and linear term in V2/3, see Table 3B, Figure 4Aii right).
evidence: Direct statement of result with reference to table and figure.

claim: Attending to vision relative to audition increased responses in regions that were activated by visual looming stimuli, yet suppressed the deactivations in the surrounding regions that were deactivated by visual stimuli.
source: Consistent with mechanisms of contrast enhancement (Bressler et al., 2013; Müller and Kleinschmidt, 2004; Smith et al., 2000; Tootell et al., 1998), attending to vision relative to audition increased responses in regions that were activated by visual looming stimuli, yet suppressed the deactivations in the surrounding regions that were deactivated by visual stimuli thereby cancelling out global attentional effects for the regional BOLD response (Figure 4Bii, note the white lines indicate the border between visual activation and deactivation from Figure 2—figure supplement 1B right).
evidence: Statement of result with citations to previous research on contrast enhancement.

claim: Auditory looming induced widespread deactivations in visual cortices that were maximal at the cortical surface and extended into regions that represent more peripheral visual fields.
source: In summary, auditory looming induced widespread deactivations in visual cortices that were maximal at the cortical surface and extended into regions that represent more peripheral visual fields.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: Attention to vision predominantly increased BOLD response in central parts that were activated by visual stimuli and suppressed BOLD responses in the periphery that were deactivated by visual stimuli.
source: By contrast, attention to vision predominantly increased BOLD response in central parts that were activated by visual stimuli and suppressed BOLD responses in the periphery that were deactivated by visual stimuli.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: Visual looming suppressed activations in auditory cortices but enhanced the response to concurrent auditory looming in posterior auditory cortices.
source: Visual looming suppressed activations in auditory cortices (see also [Laurienti et al., 2002; Leitão et al., 2013; Mozolic et al., 2008], but enhanced the response to concurrent auditory looming in posterior auditory cortices (Werner and Noppeney, 2011; Werner and Noppeney, 2010).
evidence: Statement of result with citations to previous research.

claim: Intersensory competition for purely visual stimuli turned into cooperative interactions for audiovisual stimuli.
source: In other words, intersensory competition for purely visual stimuli turned into cooperative interactions for audiovisual stimuli.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: The visual-induced response suppression was constant across cortical depth in A1 and PT.
source: While the visual-induced response suppression was constant across cortical depth in A1 and PT, the crossmodal BOLD-response enhancement was observed mainly in the caudal parts of PT, that is in parts of PT where visual influences have previously been shown (Kayser et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement of result with citation to previous research.

claim: Visual looming enhanced and suppressed auditory responses in adjacent patches consistent with neurophysiological results in non-human primates.
source: As shown in the surface projections (see Figure 3B), visual looming enhanced and suppressed auditory responses in adjacent patches consistent with neurophysiological results in non-human primates (Kayser et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement of result with citation to previous research.

claim: The large attentional BOLD-response effects in superficial laminae dovetail with previous neurophysiological research, which located effects of modality-specific attention in supragranular layers of auditory cortices.
source: The large attentional BOLD-response effects in superficial laminae dovetail nicely with previous neurophysiological research, which located effects of modality-specific attention in supragranular layers of auditory cortices (De Martino et al., 2015a; Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: Interpretation of result with citations to previous research.

claim: The GE-EPI BOLD response measured at superficial laminae includes contributions from deeper laminae.
source: Yet, because the GE-EPI BOLD response measured at superficial laminae includes contributions from deeper laminae (Harel et al., 2006; Markuerkiaga et al., 2016), we cannot unequivocally attribute the attentional influences at the cortical surface solely to superficial layers as neural origin.
evidence: Statement about methodological limitation with citations.

claim: The dissociation in laminar profiles in the same territories cannot be explained by vascular effects that limit the laminar specificity of the BOLD response, but strongly implies that multisensory and attentional mechanisms regulate information flow in auditory cortices via partly distinct neural circuitries.
source: Critically, however, the laminar profiles for attentional effects were distinct from those for multisensory (i.e. crossmodal) effects in auditory cortices. This dissociation in laminar profiles in the same territories cannot be explained by vascular effects that limit the laminar specificity of the BOLD response, but strongly implies that multisensory and attentional mechanisms regulate information flow in auditory cortices via partly distinct neural circuitries (De Martino et al., 2015a; Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citations to previous research.

claim: The constant laminar profiles for crossmodal influences in auditory cortices suggest that visual signals influence auditory cortices mainly via infragranular layers.
source: Further, the constant laminar profiles for crossmodal influences in auditory cortices suggest that visual signals influence auditory cortices mainly via infragranular layers – a finding that converges with a recent neurophysiological study in mouse that likewise highlighted deep layer six as the key locus for visual influences on auditory cortex (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citation to previous research.

claim: Anatomical studies in monkeys have suggested that visual inputs can influence auditory cortices via three routes: thalamic afferents, direct connectivity between sensory areas, and connections from higher order association cortices.
source: Anatomical studies in monkeys have previously suggested that visual inputs can influence auditory cortices via three routes (Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Musacchia and Schroeder, 2009; Schroeder et al., 2003; Smiley and Falchier, 2009): i. thalamic afferents, ii. direct connectivity between sensory areas (Falchier et al., 2002; Rockland and Ojima, 2003) and iii. connections from higher order association cortices.
evidence: Statement about anatomical pathways with citations to previous research.

claim: Visual and auditory stimuli evoked responses in visual cortices that were maximal in absolute amplitude at the cortical surface, yet differed in their activation pattern.
source: In visual cortices, visual and auditory stimuli evoked responses that were maximal in absolute amplitude at the cortical surface, yet differed in their activation pattern.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: Auditory stimuli induced widespread deactivations particularly in peripheral visual field representations known to have denser direct fibre connections to auditory cortices.
source: In contrast to this visual 'centre-surround' pattern, auditory stimuli induced widespread deactivations (Laurienti et al., 2002; Leitão et al., 2013; Mozolic et al., 2008) particularly in peripheral visual field representations known to have denser direct fibre connections to auditory cortices (Falchier et al., 2002; Rockland and Ojima, 2003).
evidence: Statement of result with citations to previous research.

claim: Both visual and auditory stimuli induced deactivations in visual cortices that were most evident at the cortical surface, as previously reported for deactivations to ipsilateral visual stimuli.
source: In visual cortices, both visual and auditory stimuli induced deactivations that were most evident at the cortical surface, as previously reported for deactivations to ipsilateral visual stimuli (Fracasso et al., 2018), though see [Goense et al., 2012].
evidence: Statement of result with citations to previous research.

claim: Neurophysiological studies in rodents have shown asymmetries in multisensory influences between auditory and visual cortices, reporting robust auditory induced inhibition in layers 2/3 in visual cortices but not visual-induced inhibition in auditory cortices.
source: For instance, neurophysiological studies in rodents have shown asymmetries in multisensory influences between auditory and visual cortices, reporting robust auditory induced inhibition in layers 2/3 in visual cortices but not visual-induced inhibition in auditory cortices (Iurilli et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about previous research with citation.

claim: The differences in activation patterns for multisensory and attentional influences indicate that the impact of purely auditory looming on visual cortices cannot solely be attributed to a withdrawal of attentional resources from vision.
source: The differences in activation patterns for multisensory and attentional influences indicate that the impact of purely auditory looming (Maier et al., 2008; Maier et al., 2004) on visual cortices cannot solely be attributed to a withdrawal of attentional resources from vision.
evidence: Interpretation of results with citations to previous research.

claim: Purely auditory looming may inhibit activations in visual cortices via direct connectivity between auditory and visual areas.
source: Instead, purely auditory looming may inhibit activations in visual cortices via direct connectivity between auditory and visual areas (Bizley et al., 2007; Budinger et al., 2006; Campi et al., 2010; Falchier et al., 2002; Ibrahim et al., 2016; Rockland and Ojima, 2003).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to previous research on connectivity.

claim: Research in rodents has shown that auditory stimuli modulates activity in supragranular layers in primary visual areas via direct connectivity from auditory cortices and translaminar inhibitory circuits.
source: In line with this conjecture, research in rodents has shown that auditory stimuli modulates activity in supragranular layers in primary visual areas via direct connectivity from auditory cortices and translaminar inhibitory circuits – though the studies disagreed in whether layer 5 (Iurilli et al., 2012) or layer 1 (Deneux et al., 2019; Ibrahim et al., 2016) were the primary targets of auditory inputs.
evidence: Statement about previous research with citations.

claim: The study reveals distinct laminar profiles for multisensory deactivations in auditory and visual cortices.
source: Our results reveal distinct laminar profiles for multisensory deactivations in auditory and visual cortices.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: In auditory cortices the visual induced deactivations were constant across laminae, in visual cortices the deactivations linearly increased (in absolute magnitude) toward cortical surface.
source: In auditory cortices the visual induced deactivations were constant across laminae, in visual cortices the deactivations linear increased (in absolute magnitude) toward cortical surface.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: These distinct laminar profiles converge with previous research in rodents that reveal visual influences in auditory cortices predominantly in infragranular layer, but auditory influences in visual cortices mainly in supragranular layers.
source: These distinct laminar profiles converge with previous research in rodents that also reveal visual influences in auditory cortices predominantly in infragranular layer (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018), but auditory influences in visual cortices mainly in supragranular layers (Deneux et al., 2019; Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012).
evidence: Interpretation of results with citations to previous research.

claim: The distinct laminar profiles across cortical areas may reflect differences in neural circuitries or differences in vascular organization.
source: Potentially, these distinct laminar profiles in auditory and visual cortices may suggest that multisensory influences are mediated by different neural circuitries in auditory and visual cortices. However, the distinct laminar profiles across cortical areas may not only reflect differences in neural circuitries but also in vascular organization.
evidence: Interpretation with acknowledgment of alternative explanations.

claim: Multisensory responses profoundly depend on stimulus salience and other input characteristics.
source: Moreover, a wealth of research has previously shown that multisensory responses profoundly depend on stimulus salience and other input characteristics (Deneux et al., 2019; Meijer et al., 2017; Stein et al., 2020; Werner and Noppeney, 2010).
evidence: Statement about previous research with citations.

claim: It is currently unclear how stimulus salience and other input characteristics influence laminar BOLD-response profiles.
source: It is currently unclear how these factors influence laminar BOLD-response profiles.
evidence: Statement about current knowledge gap.

claim: Interpreting laminar BOLD-response profiles in relation to previous findings in rodents remains tentative because of cross-species and methodological differences.
source: Finally, interpreting laminar BOLD-response profiles in relation to previous findings in rodents remains tentative because of cross-species and methodological differences.
evidence: Statement about limitations of interpretation.

claim: In visual cortices auditory stimulation induced widespread inhibition, while attention to vision enhanced central but suppressed peripheral field representations.
source: In visual cortices auditory stimulation induced widespread inhibition, while attention to vision enhanced central but suppressed peripheral field representations.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: In auditory cortices, competitive and cooperative multisensory interactions were stronger deep within the cortex, while attentional influences were greatest at the cortical surface.
source: In auditory cortices, competitive and cooperative multisensory interactions were stronger deep within the cortex, while attentional influences were greatest at the cortical surface.
evidence: Summary statement of result.

claim: The distinctiveness of depth-dependent activation profiles and patterns suggests that multisensory and attentional mechanisms control information flow via partly distinct neural circuitries.
source: The distinctiveness of these depth-dependent activation profiles and patterns suggests that multisensory and attentional mechanisms control information flow via partly distinct neural circuitries.
evidence: Interpretation of overall findings.
